title: The Four Registers of the Proprium and the Turning Wheel of Purification
reading:
There is a great work that the Lord has set within the soul, and it is plain to anyone who looks: the recurrent turning by which states are purified, again and again, in freedom. This turning is one among four registers in which the proprium has been distributed and held — four registers in which the soul's claiming is permitted to take its forms, so that the rational may be formed at all and yet not collapse under what it has claimed.

The first register is the powers held above, in the ten ordered degrees of the rational; the soul's self-loving arrangements are bound there, gathered into those upper degrees and held in their place.

The second register is the natural mind below — the ground on which we walk and everything beneath it: the natural taken in its lower aspects, joined to the four places where the proprium has its deepest hold.

The third register is the settled disorders that ring the natural mind round about — the strongholds and fortifications that self-love builds for itself, with the principalities and powers it has gathered into them.

The fourth register is the recurrent circuit itself — the turning of states under which the soul passes again and again. This is heavy with shame and concupiscence; for the firstborn shapes of the proprium and all its chief principalities, which once stood proud in the third register, have been bound, gathered, reckoned, fixed into this turning, hung opposite one another in a single accord, and set to revolve. They could not be bound above — the higher degrees could not bear them. They could not be fixed below in the natural's mountains — those could not bear them either. So the Lord set them upon this revolving cycle, so that the good and truth which rise from the lower degrees might be received as they pass through, lifted, and given upward; and so that what falls from above — whether in the cold of withholding or the heat of trial — might be carried by the same revolution and cast over the whole natural ground, the whole tree of perception, until every part has had its share in the work.

For consider what the proprium is: it is like a king who has reigned to seize a kingship for himself, gathered around him a great train of strivings — all the principalities of self-rule, the whole garment of contention, the love of strife, the multitudes that crowd his court, the fair likeness he has fashioned, the desires he has drawn into himself, the property and the affections that issued from his hunger to possess. The king is the measure of his whole train; the train is the measure of his whole reign; nothing comes forth before his face — neither victory nor command — that is not his whole kingship at once, in such wisdom and skill and judgment as he has.

So it is with the proprium organized through this turning. The whole work of self-love is gathered into the recurrent cycle, into the seven leaders that move it, into the twelve fixed states the soul passes through; and all its settled disorders are gathered to its king, gathered to the way-leaders that drive the formation of the natural mind. Whatever is reckoned in the soul's outer world or inner — the strifes, the disturbances, the soul's self-binding, the hunger, the desire, the property it multiplies and the property it loses — all of it is moved through these way-leaders. They move the whole formation; the whole work is gathered into them.

This is the shape of what the soul has claimed: held in four registers, turned in a cycle so that what cannot yet be borne above or below is borne in the revolving, and so that influx rising and influx falling have a path through which to do their work upon the whole.
